narrative:

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your LSAT score had the strongest influence and pushed the prediction toward failure. At 32, it sits noticeably below the average of 37 among students who were admitted, signaling weaker preparation in the eyes of the model. Your undergraduate GPA came next and worked in your favor, pulling the prediction slightly toward passing; however, at 2.70 it remains well below the 3.23 average of accepted students, limiting how much it could offset the LSAT effect. Your third-year class ranking followed closely behind. A decile of 4 also pulled the outcome modestly toward success, yet it still lags the 5.79 average of admitted peers, so its positive effect was not strong enough to change the result.

Taken together, these academic signals led the model to conclude your risk of failing the bar was slightly more than even. To improve your chances, focus on raising your LSAT score through targeted preparation, as this carries the greatest weight. Strengthening your class rank in future years and boosting your GPA where possible will also help demonstrate readiness. Consider reapplying once these areas show clear progress.
